projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Howard Hall was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: We are here today with Mr. Howard Hall. His birth date was July 17, 1916. He served in World War II.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What? What time did you say, 7-16?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Was that your birth date?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: July 17th.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yes, sir. He was in the U.S. Army. The highest rank achieved was a colonel in the Army Reserve. Today is November 11, 2009, and we are in Des Moines, Iowa. I am Bethany Wright. Our court reporter with us today is Sheryl Currier, and our videographer is Kathy Block. The interview is being conducted for the Veteran's History Project at the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Pretty easy so far, huh?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Pretty easy so far. Pretty easy so far?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, I'm all right.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I think. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: No, you're fine. I'll ask you a few questions --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- about where -- about your bio-- about your biographical history.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: So where and when were you born?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Uh, July 17, 1916, in -- in --

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Williams.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Williams, Iowa.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Would you like to tell me about your family.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: About my family? Well, what do you want to know? Uh, my father came from Norway, and then he married my mother, who was in this -- was in this country. And that's it.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Are you an only child?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No. There's -- there were four of us. Three of them are dead, except me.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Were you the only one who served --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- in the service? Were you the only one in the service?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Well, moved from here to there. I went to -- when I was drafted, I went to Fort Belvoir, take training, I mean, take --

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: For your --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: And I was commissioned. And went into service then as a Second Lieutenant -- I mean, I was in the service already, but -- and let's see, yeah. And sometime -- I forget -- about a year later, I got promoted to First Lieutenant, and that's where I stayed. Wasn't good enough.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did other members of your family --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did other members of your family serve in the military?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Just you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Just me.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: What year did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What year did I enlist? I didn't enlist. I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Oh, you were drafted. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I, uh, I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: '43. Yeah, I think -- I think it was '43. I should have taken my discharge with me.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: They have a copy.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, did they? Oh, they do.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: October 14th, 1942.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. That's about right.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: What do you remember about departing for training camp?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: For training camp? I don't really remember anything much about it. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: That's okay. Can you tell me about adapting to military life?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: About what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Adapting to military life?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: About how you felt going into the military?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: How I liked it?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Didn't like it. Never did like it.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: It was really hard to leave your family, I bet?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: The only thing is, I stayed in it afterwards and stayed in the reserves, ended up retired with a Lieutenant Colonel. So now I've got income coming from that.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did you -- You did go abroad; correct?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I did go where?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Abroad? You went oversees?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Can you tell me about that?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Japan. We went over -- Well, we went down to the Philippines, and let's see, Philippines. Went to Hawaii first, and then to the Philippines, and then to Japan.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Didn't you stop at Pelilieu and Anwar on the way?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Didn't you fight at Pelilieu and Anwar on the way?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: On the way?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Well, we went on board ship. We were supposed to land and spent 45 more days more on board ship while we were waiting to land. I'm not much help.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Oh, no, you're great. You're great. Can you tell me -- Can you tell me about your duties?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: About your duties?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What I ate?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: No, about, about your role?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What did I do?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: On board ship? Well, I did a little training, not much, but just went up and down the ship, had meals. The enlisted men ate separately, then, from the officers. That's about all I can remember.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I see here that you were a combat engineer.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Combat engineer?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: You were in the combat engineers?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, combat engineers. Yeah. Excuse me, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: That's okay. And you were a platoon leader?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: You were a platoon leader?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: You were the leader of the platoon?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. Yep. Yep, I was. A lot of that service, I kind of -- I think I put it out of my mind. It wasn't fun. I didn't like it.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Can you tell me about friendships that you formed --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- while you were in the military, the camaraderie?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, I had some very good friends. I had some very nice -- seemed like. Of course, as an officer, I had friends, but it was really nice. Had nice friends. They were all from the same sort of thing, so --

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: They were all drafted as well?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Were you able to do anything recreational off duty?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did you do anything -- Were you able to do anything for fun off duty, when you were off duty?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Just all business?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Where were you when your tour of duty ended?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Where was I what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: When your tour of duty ended, when you came home?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Came in to, let's see, I went in -- let me think, just -- I came into -- let's see. Well, on the west coast. I was thinking I came in on -- huh, Portland. I'm not sure. I can't remember that.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: That's okay. Was there any kind of reception held for you --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- or for your platoon?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No, except my wife.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: And your son?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: That was really about it. That was very good. And he was born during the war.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How did you adjust to coming home?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How did you adjust to coming home after being at war?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I was so happy. I don't know, but I don't know how I adapted.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Just happy to be home?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. I don't remember much about it. I really don't.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did you go right into the reserves?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No. I stayed in the reserves, and that was a nice thing. Wouldn't have been nice if I would have been called back to service.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: But luckily you never were?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Do you keep in contact with fellow veterans --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- that you served with? Do you still talk to fellow veterans that you served with?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, some of them. Was another man by the name of Hall that was from the west coast. He was my company commander at one time. Good man because his name was Hall (laughter). Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Are you a member of any veteran's organizations?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No. Nope. Nope.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How did these experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: How did they expect (sic) my -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Being drafted?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I really don't know. Probably was good for me. I don't know. But I don't know.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Can you tell me any life lessons that you learned from the military?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Can I tell you any what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Lessons, life lessons?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Anything that it, that it taught you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I don't remember. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: There's a lot of things -- I think I tried to put a lot of that stuff out about what it was like, so I've kind of forgotten a lot of it.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: It wasn't the happiest days.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I see here that you were awarded the Asiatic- Pacific Theatre Service Ribbon --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- with two Bronze Stars, the Philippine Liberation Ribbon with one Bronze Star, and the Purple Heart.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What about the Purple Heart? The Purple Heart. That's when I made a mistake trying to blast some Japanese out of the cave below me. I got it over the edge. Went off too soon. Got my ears. That sent me home (laughter).

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: That's what the letter was about --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- that's -- that's included here --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- that you had written when you were in the hospital --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- after the injuries to your ears.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. Guadalcanal. Let's see. Yep. Yep. He probably knows more about it than I do.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Do we want to read the letter into the record maybe?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Sure can.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Would that be okay, Mr. Hall --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- if I read your letter into, into the record?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No, that would be all right. You can if you want to.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Sir, would you like to read it?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Okay. Maybe I can read it. "November 18, 1944. Dear Harold and Annie. No, you didn't have my correct address on your letter as you can see from this envelope. But it certainly wasn't your fault, as I suddenly changed addresses about two weeks ago without any forewarning at all. The army, though, is rather good at getting the mail to one sooner or later, and yesterday I received my first mail since landing in this place. It consisted of your letter and one from Berniece --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Hmmm.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: -- both very welcome, let me assure you. Mail is about all one really looks forward to over here, except, of course, for the end of the war. And the latter appears to be quite away off, at least to me. You're probably wondering what occurred that I should be here. Well, here's the tale.

My platoon and I were busy aiding the infantry trying to clean out some Japs out of a pocket we had them in on Peleliu in the Palau Islands. There was one sniper that was giving us quite a bit of trouble from a cave he was hidden in. I decided to drop a charge (221/2 pounds of explosive) from the top of the hill to the mouth of the cave by the use of old telephone wire and there detonate it. From where I was, I couldn't see it (the cave), so I had a man on the adjacent ridge watching, prepared to signal when I got it in place. With the aid of my sergeant, I prepared the charge, making the mistake (as I look back on it) of using a delay detonator, planning to set it off when I got it where I wanted it. I threw it over the side of the cliff and started to lower it. The detonator caught and went off when I wasn't expecting it, about ten feet away. That sort of shook me up, and I crawled back to a safer spot to see if anyone had been hurt. Everyone said they were all right. I was sort of deaf, about like when a firecracker goes off in your hand.

So I ordered another pack and lowered it over the side with plans to detonate it in a different manner. My man signaled when it was in place. About that time, I discovered a lightening of my line attached to the pack. The little yellow monkey had snipped it by cutting my lines with a knife before they could shoot him. That really got under my hide, though you can see his point of view.

Again I got another pack. This time I told my man I wanted to know when it was a foot above the opening. We got it there without any more trouble and set it off. I think that sort of started the Nip on his way to join the "honorable ancestors". At least he didn't bother us any more.

So feeling relieved that that job was done, I went back to the C.P. and reported. While there, I had the Doc at the aid station look at my ears. He didn't seem to think there was anything the matter, so I went back to work. Shortly afterwards, the company commander came around, and I told him I thought I better go back to the company as I didn't feel much like working. He agreed. There I went to our medical officer, and he took me to the hospital. There they said I had two perforated ear drums and would have to stay. They evacuated me here, and I guess here I will stay until I am well again.

As for feeling all right, I've been feeling well except for a few earaches and a clogged-up feeling in my head. Actually, on the whole, I felt so well it has sort of seemed silly to be in the hospital, but I guess these medics know their business. By the way, those fellows deserve a lot of credit for their great work, from the aide men all the way back. They've done excellent work, and the men give them a lot of praise, which they deserve.

Time out while I light up a cigar. They are plentiful here at the P.X., and they were a luxury where I came from. Now, where was I? I guess I was discussing how I felt. I am partially deaf, but the Doc says I'll regain all my hearing if things aren't any worse than he thinks they are. That is something I am thankful for. How long it will take, I don't know, and he doesn't seem to either. Time will have to tell us that.

My treatment consists of seeing the Doc each morning and putting drops in my ears three or four times a day. Otherwise, I've got life easy. I've got a very comfortable bed, and don't think it doesn't feel good after sleeping on the ground and in some rather rocky foxholes for a couple of months. And it has sheets.

Now, of course, I'm getting used to it. The chow is good -- steak about once a week and ice cream about the same number of times. There's a P.X. where we can get little items -- though nothing like those in the States. I can wander about all over the area, and it's a rather nice spot. The ocean is only 100 feet away -- 100 feet from the front door and has a beautiful beach.

Some of the patients go swimming, but I don't, due to my ears and the lack of ambition. Yes, I'm definitely getting lazy. They have shows about four times a week. (Good ones, too. Last night was "Casanova Brown".) I could hear if I get up close enough to the screen.

They also have some Red Cross workers here come through and ask if we wanted anything. They have a recreation building a short ways from this ward. I had heard about these Red Cross girls before, but this is the first I had seen them out here. I don't know whether they are of value or not, but some of the fellows enjoy having them come around. I'll admit, it was nice to see a white woman again. They also have nurses here, and a few are really easy on the eyes.

I have yet to speak to one, though, as they seem to work only with the worst cases, and there's plenty of them. I get a kick out of some of the officers who try to play up to some of these nurses. They get cut off rather short -- They get cut off rather short, and I secretly think it hurts the pride of some of them.

You know I get rather bitter and sore at times when I read about fellows back in the States worrying about higher wages and striking to get them. It seems they can forget that for a while and concentrate on winding up this war. Yet, if I were one of them, I would probably do the same thing. That seems the human nature. We always want more than we have, and at times, it's a very good thing.

But I do feel some (or should I say a lot of) people don't seem to realize there's a war on. I may be pessimistic, but I think we still have a couple years in this theater, and the going from now is going to be much rougher than it has been. My hope is when it is finally over, that they will have -- they will find some sort of a peace that will last for quite a number of years.

I really have very little hope of a lasting permanent peace. I don't need to tell you that war isn't a glorious thing. Perhaps you wonder how I felt when I saw the dead for the first time. Strange as it may seem, the dead Japs affected me about like a dead horse or pig. The American dead made me feel a bit angry at the whole thing. Very seldom did I think much when looking at a dead Jap soldier. Once in a while I'd wonder what his home was like, if he had a family, etc, but it's best not to think of that when one is fighting. I never really could blame them for things and the war.

It was the military caste in Tokyo who I really felt and feel strongly against. They were the ones who are responsible. They fed the people propaganda, and how were they not to know it wasn't the truth? But let me assure you, there's no love lost between the Jap soldier and the American. It's usually one or the other when they meet. And our men are good. I've got a lot of respect for some men and the things I've seen them do.

Now, look at what I've written. I hope you don't get too bored. If you do, you can always quit. I just started writing and kept on. You mentioned not having much time in your letter. Well, I have plenty of it here. About all I do is read and sleep and eat. I wish I could join you in your hunting. I'd get a bang out of going out with some of the old gang again. Not so much for the game that was shot, but for the razzings that everyone got. A good bunch of fellows!

How about shells? Aren't they hard to get? And bowling. I've often thought of that. I'd get a big kick out of bowling another game with you, Alvin, Mike, Sasor Geane, and some of the others. Alvin used to tickle me so when he got so disgusted. Those were enjoyable times. I wonder if we will all ever get together again. It would be nice; though, naturally things would be different.

I've rattled enough for this time. I hope you don't have too hard of a time with my penmanship. It seems to have continued to grow worse since I left high school. Good luck to both of you and my very best wishes. Write when you aren't too busy. As ever, Howard.
P.S. Merry Christmas --" This shouldn't be hard for me. "-- It's a bit early, but it may be too late later on. May the new year see a return of this unsettled world to peace."

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Thank you. Thank you for reading that.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: That was a lot harder than I thought it was going to be.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: We're so glad that you were able to come also. That was written November 18th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: You wrote that November 18th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I wasn't what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: The letter that your son just read --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- was written by you in 1944.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh. Oh. Yeah. Yep.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Thank you for reading that.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: That was a wonderful thing, those letters coming.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I bet. To get mail from your loved ones from home.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, And I got a lot of them. And mail call was a big thing.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Who were Harold and Annie to you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Your letter was addressed to Harold and Annie?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: My mail -- my mother was what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Your letter here was addressed to Harold and Annie.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Who, who were they to you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: That's cousin. Cousin. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Were they friends of yours?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Did they sign it?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Were they friends?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: How did you know them?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: (No response.)

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Dad, how did you know them?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Know what?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Harold.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: He went to high school with me.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: He -- let's see. He was a senior in high school, and I was a junior. Went to big town Hanlontown. 49 students in the high school (laughter). Yeah. Anything else I can do for you?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Is there anything else you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Okay. Did your son reading this letter, did it bring up any other memories for you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: It brought up some. I -- probably if I looked at it longer, bring up more. But it, yeah, it brought up some.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Any that you would like to share with us?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Anything you would like to share for the interview?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No, not in particular.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I don't remember some of that stuff in detail enough to --

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I probably remember it wrong. But, no, I don't want to do that.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Well, thank you so much, Howard Hall, for your time.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Did your ears after your hospital stay, did they ever recover? Did you ever fully gain your hearing back?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: They recovered for a while, and then kept getting worse. And they, uh -- Let's see. Let me think about that. Oh, they got worse and worse, and then I applied -- Well, not applied. They gave me a test down at the VA, and they said I needed hearing aids, and they gave the kind of hearing aids that you stuck in like that. These are so much better than those.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Um, you ask so many questions. Okay. Let's see. I would say probably only about five years ago.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How did you feel when you found out that your son was born when you were oversees?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, I wasn't overseas. He was born here.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Just before he left.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Oh, okay. So he was just a baby when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: But, uh, when he was born, I had been out on the firing range all day. I was so tired, I could hardly stay awake. They called my wife in when she had -- was going to have the baby, called her in, and they came out and say, "You had your son."

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: They woke you up.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Any other children?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Any other children?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Just one son?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: He's the baby of the family. Yeah (laughter). No, I didn't have any other. That was -- I can't remember where I was going. I was going some place. Are you learning some things?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Not a lot. You had been -- You were so tired you could hardly stay awake when I was -- when mom was in labor.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: And they did wake him up when --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I went to sleep. I was so tired, I'd been on the firing range, and had fired all day. Came back, and they said that she was in the hospital, and that they wouldn't, you know, wouldn't let you in at that time, and I was out in the chairs. I had gone to sleep. And there was the doctor saying, "You have a boy."

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: So how old were you -- or how old was your son when you returned?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: How old was I, Brian?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: No, no, how old was I when you got back?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: How old was he when I got back?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: When you left.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Well, about -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: I was born in February. When did you ship out?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I could figure them out maybe.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I think, did it say April?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah, I think it's April. So I was about two months old at that point.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: And then the separation date was February 21st, 1946.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: So you would have been four?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: I would have been two.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Oh, I see. He was already -- had already been drafted when you were --

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I guess my wife forgave me for going to sleep (laughter).

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Well, she does mention it sometimes.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: That being -- that being on the firing range all day, it was a hard job because you had to go back and forth, watch these fellows shoot, and we went out early in the morning and came back late at night. It was rough. And there he was. Anything else? I didn't plan to get questioned all this way.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Ha, ha. It's good for you.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: In your history, it talked about that you were responsible for --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: -- that you supervised and directed the conconstruction of roads and bridges, mine fields, that you demolished bridges. Do you remember that or can you talk about that?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Mine lines, mine fields? Yeah. I remember them. Had to be very careful. Lucky I never got hurt. Neither did anybody else that I knew.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: How about the colonel that wanted to drive the bulldozer?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: How about the colonel who wanted to drive the bulldozer?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I can't remember just exactly. He was going to ride the bulldozer, and he didn't know how to handle it. He wanted to learn how.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: So you taught him?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: So did you teach him?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No. I couldn't ride it. There was another guy who was riding, driving that bulldozer. It was a handy weapon, bulldozer was.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: What made it a weapon? What made the bulldozer a weapon?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Nothing, except the fact that it had the big blade and could push this drift up and stuff. That's about all it did. It pushed it up and gave you protection. It had this big blade in the front. It helped. This isn't the kind of stuff I like to remember.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Is there anything else that you can think of that we should ask?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Not that I know about.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Is there anything else, Mr. Hall, that you would like to share with us?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Anything else about your service that you would like to share with us today?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No. I can't really say anything.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Well, we appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: It's funny how much I've lost that remains -- I think I finally -- I just put it away, but I don't remember a lot of it. I remember trying to find my way out to the coast and almost got lost. Then I had to come through --California had a -- you had to go through this entrance at that time. I don't know why. But anyway. Didn't take long. You just -- In fact, we came, and they kind of knew who we were, and they let us through.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How did you travel to California?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: How were you traveling?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Truck.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I remember my, my grandfather was a World War II vet, and I remember him telling stories about hitchhiking to California.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: How did he go? Did he go by truck?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: He hitchhiked.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh. Oh, yeah. We had a company -- we had, I think, one truck for each -- for each -- let's see, what did they call them? Anyway, they -- we had these trucks, and they let us through right away, but they -- For some reason or another I can't figure out why we had -- we were sus -- I mean, we were checked. But I don't know why. That's a long time ago.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: I think at that time --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: About sixty years ago.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: It's a little more.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: I think California had a concern with the agricultural contamination, things coming in from other parts of the country, and that's why they had their blockade. They still had that in the '60s, early '60s.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, they, they shipped the trunks, some of them. I mean, they would ship your trunk. They lost mine. So I had a platoon sergeant who was classified as a carpenter, and he built me one, and I have it at home. I'm rather proud of it.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Good work.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Thank you so much, Howard Hall, for sharing your story with us today.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Well, you're sure welcome. I wish I could remember better things. I don't..

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: No, you don't.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yes, I -- Some of it I do. Most of it, I kind of think you try to put some of this stuff away. War is not fun --

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Thank you for your service.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: -- especially when they shoot against you. I didn't get into that much of that because I was with the engineers and we built the bridges and stuff like that, so it was very little combat that I saw, actually saw. I remember building a bridge across the river and something like that, but it was -- It wasn't really a good bridge span, but -- SHERYL CURRIER: Didn't the war end shortly after that letter?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Yes, but the war in the Pacific went on beyond that. And then you served some time in occupied Japan, too, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Weren't you in occupied Japan for a while? Weren't you in Japan for a while after?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Weren't you --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: I never had any music.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: No, no, no. Weren't you in occupied Japan after the war --

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: -- after the fighting?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I got into military government and was there for quite a while. That was nice. Because there was only two of us in the outfit did the work we did, and I liked it. But I was ready to go home. That was about four years, I think, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Pretty close you were there.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Anyway --

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Okay. I think we're done here.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: I think we're done.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bethanie Wright
sp.p: Are you ready to be done?

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Isn't it fun to sit here and question people?

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: I think we're finished unless you've got something else.

sp.speaker: Howard Hall
sp.p: Okay. I'm ready.

sp.speaker: Brian Hall
sp.p: Okay. I thought you would be.
